ideas.title: You advise others better than yourself
ideas.idea: People reason more wisely about other people's problems than about their own. In 2014 the psychologists Igor Grossmann and Ethan Kross named this Solomon's paradox, after the biblical king who judged everyone's disputes brilliantly yet, the legend goes, handled his own household badly. The gap isn't about intelligence or age. When we are inside a problem, we see it from the first-person view: we fixate on how it feels, and we find it hard to see other possibilities or admit what we don't know. The remedy turned out to be cheap. Think about your own situation as an outside observer would, for example by describing it using your own name or 'he' or 'she' instead of 'I'. In the experiments, this small shift in language closed the gap, so people reasoned about their own troubles as wisely as they did about a friend's.
ideas.deep_dive:
Grossmann and Kross's paper, 'Exploring Solomon's Paradox', appeared in Psychological Science in 2014 and reported three experiments with 693 participants in all. In the first, people imagined a partner cheating on them, or a friend's partner cheating on the friend. They then wrote about it and were scored on features of wise reasoning: recognising the limits of their own knowledge, seeing that circumstances can change, considering other perspectives, and looking for compromise. Those thinking about someone else's predicament scored higher than those thinking about their own.

The later studies tested a fix. Some participants were asked to take a distanced stance, reflecting on their own situation as an observer would, or referring to themselves by name and with third-person pronouns. That removed the gap. The effect held across younger and older adults, which is notable because wisdom is often assumed to rise simply with age. It seems to depend as much on where you stand when you think as on how much experience you have.

This fits a wider programme of work by Kross's lab on 'distanced self-talk'. In a 2014 paper in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology (seven experiments, 585 participants), people who spoke to themselves using their name or 'you' ahead of a stressful speech did better, according to independent raters, and showed less distress and less brooding afterwards.

The limits: the wisdom scores come from what people write in a lab, not from what they later do. The studies mostly used relationship scenarios. And distancing isn't a magic wand; it helps you reflect, but it can't supply facts you don't have.

examples.title: The imagined affair, yours or a friend's
examples.text: In Grossmann and Kross's first experiment, participants considered a partner's infidelity. Half pictured it happening in their own relationship, half in a friend's. Both groups answered questions that were scored for wise reasoning, such as whether they recognised uncertainty, expected change over time and could see the other person's view. Those thinking about a friend's situation scored significantly higher than those thinking about their own. The same event, with only the owner changed, produced noticeably more balanced thinking. It is the clearest demonstration that the difficulty lies in being immersed, not in lacking the knowledge.

examples.title: Speaking about yourself by name before a speech
examples.text: In a 2014 study led by Kross, students were given a short time to prepare a speech on why they were qualified for their dream job, to be judged by others. Some were told to prepare using the first-person 'I'; others used their own name or 'you'. According to the paper's abstract, the non-first-person group was rated as performing better by objective raters, showed less distress, and ruminated less afterwards. A tiny change in pronouns, made in private before a real public performance, changed how it went.

examples.title: Writing about Ebola by name in 2014
examples.text: During the October 2014 Ebola scare, Kross and colleagues recruited 1,257 Americans and asked them to write about their feelings on the outbreak, using either 'I' or their own name. Among people who began with high worry, those writing in the third person produced more fact-based reasons not to be worried, and those reasons predicted lower worry and lower perceived risk. The result is an everyday case: a public anxiety eased not by new information but by looking at it from a step back.

images.caption: Rubens's workshop painting of the Judgement of Solomon, the story that gave the paradox its name.
images.credit: Peter Paul Rubens (workshop) / public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

why: Three experiments (693 people) found the self-other gap and its removal by distancing, in both younger and older adults; the speech and Ebola studies come from the same lab, so independent replication matters.
Caveat: the results are from lab writing tasks, mostly about relationships, and measure how wisely people reason, not how they later behave.
ideas.try_this: Next time you're stuck on a decision, write two sentences about it in the third person, using your own name ("Phil is torn because..."), then ask what you would tell a friend in the same position.

ideas.title: Adding a road can slow everyone down
ideas.idea: Braess's paradox is the discovery that adding a new route to a network can make every user's journey slower. It sounds impossible, because more capacity should never hurt. But it can, when each person picks the route that is best for them alone. Take 4,000 drivers choosing between two routes that each include one fixed 45-minute stretch and one stretch that takes the number of cars divided by 100 minutes. They split evenly and everyone takes 65 minutes. Now add a free shortcut linking the two variable stretches. Every driver switches to use both, because it looks quicker, but the variable stretches are now jammed and the trip takes 80 minutes. Nobody has a reason to go back, so everyone stays worse off. The lesson reaches well beyond traffic: in any system where people optimise for themselves, more options can quietly lower the result for all.
ideas.deep_dive:
The German mathematician Dietrich Braess published the result in 1968, while working in Münster. The underlying insight is older: Wikipedia credits Arthur Pigou in 1920 with an early version of the idea about selfish routing. Braess showed it with a small network and simple arithmetic, which is why the example survives in textbooks.

Here is the mechanism. Before the shortcut, each route has a 45-minute fixed leg and a congestible leg taking T/100 minutes, where T is the number of cars using it. With 4,000 drivers split 2,000 and 2,000, each congestible leg takes 20 minutes, so every journey takes 65. Add a free link joining the two junctions, and a single driver can pair the two congestible legs, avoiding both 45-minute legs. If everyone does so, each congestible leg now carries 4,000 cars, 40 minutes each, and the trip takes 80. A driver who returns to a 45-minute route would face 45 plus 40, which is 85, so nobody switches back. This is a Nash equilibrium: stable, but worse than before.

The conditions matter. The effect appears only for certain mixes of congestible and fixed links and certain levels of demand. At very light or very heavy traffic the new road helps or does nothing. It also relies on drivers choosing selfishly and freely, which is why it can be undone by changing the incentives (a toll) as well as by removing the road.

It is a real feature of networks, not a trick: it shows up wherever flows follow individual choices, including data networks and power grids.

examples.title: Stuttgart, 1969: closing the new road
examples.text: A widely retold case from the era of Braess's paper comes from Stuttgart, Germany. In 1969 the city invested in road building to ease traffic, but the Plus Maths article on the paradox, and other accounts, report that congestion did not improve until a newly built section of road was closed to traffic again. It is one of the earliest reported cases of the effect in a real city, although the details of the traffic counts are not widely published, so it is best read as a well-known illustration rather than a controlled test.

examples.title: Seoul replaces a highway with a stream
examples.text: Early in the 2000s Seoul removed the elevated Cheonggye Expressway and restored the Cheonggyecheon stream beneath it as a five-mile park. Officials had expected the change to worsen congestion, according to a Cornell University networks course blog, yet traffic flow in the surrounding area improved. Other changes, including public transport improvements, happened at the same time, so Seoul does not prove Braess's paradox on its own. It does show that taking away a major road does not automatically produce gridlock.

examples.title: Boston, London and New York could close roads
examples.text: In 2008 Hyejin Youn, Michael Gastner and Hawoong Jeong published a study in Physical Review Letters that modelled the road networks of Boston, London and New York. They found individual drivers waste up to 30%, 24% and 28% of their travel time compared with the best arrangement for everyone, and that closing particular roads could reduce delays: six candidates in Boston, seven in London and twelve in New York. These are model results using simplified assumptions, not trials.

examples.title: 42nd Street on Earth Day
examples.text: In 1990, New York City closed 42nd Street to traffic for Earth Day. According to accounts citing the New York Times reporter Gina Kolata, officials feared chaos but congestion in the area actually eased. It's an example anyone who has seen a street closure can picture: the expected jam never forms, because drivers re-route to a pattern that works better for the whole network.

images.caption: The two-route example with and without a shortcut, alongside a spring-and-rope version that shows the same effect mechanically.
images.credit: Cmglee, via Wikimedia Commons (licence on the file page)

images.caption: The Cheonggyecheon stream in central Seoul, restored where an expressway once ran.
images.credit: Basile Morin, via Wikimedia Commons (licence on the file page)

why: The arithmetic is exact and has been reproduced in many studies of networks; real-world confirmation is patchier and mostly consists of case studies and model results.
Caveat: it needs particular network shapes and traffic levels, so it doesn't mean fewer roads are always better.
ideas.try_this: Think of a process at work or home where you added a step, tool or option and everything got slower. Would removing it help? Ask who is choosing selfishly and what they'd choose if the option weren't there.

ideas.title: Your future self is almost a stranger
ideas.idea: The philosopher Derek Parfit argued that being the same person over time is a matter of degree, not an all-or-nothing fact. Your connection to who you were at ten, or who you will be at seventy, is a chain of memories, intentions and character that thins out with distance. If that is right, a distant future self has something in common with another person, and we may treat them accordingly: we are often generous to strangers we can see and stingy towards a future self we can't. Psychologists later took this up as a practical question. Hal Hershfield and colleagues found that people who feel more continuous with their future selves save more, and that making the future self feel real, by showing people an age-progressed picture of themselves, led them to put more aside. The philosophy gives the puzzle; the experiments suggest a lever.
ideas.deep_dive:
Parfit developed his view in Reasons and Persons (1984). He rejected the idea that personal identity is a deep further fact over and above the physical and psychological continuities between your earlier and later states. Those continuities come in degrees: your memories, intentions and personality link you to yesterday's self strongly and to your self thirty years ahead only weakly. Parfit drew a moral from this. If we care little about ourselves in the more distant future, our future selves resemble future generations, as Hershfield and colleagues note when quoting his writing. He also described how changing his own view felt: his life had seemed like a glass tunnel, moving faster each year, and the walls of the tunnel disappeared when he stopped believing in a deep further fact about identity.

The psychological work turns that into something measurable. Ersner-Hershfield, Wimmer and Knutson (2009) scanned people while they judged traits of their current and future selves, and found that differences in activity in a brain region called the rostral anterior cingulate predicted how steeply they discounted future rewards a week later. A separate self-report study found people who felt more similar to their future selves held more retirement assets, though the authors note causation could run either way, since being financially secure may itself make you feel more continuous with your future self.

The limits: you can't conclude from Parfit that you should ignore your future self. His own conclusion was that the strong dividing lines we draw between people are less deep than they seem, which cuts both ways. And the experimental effects, though real, are measured on hypothetical or small decisions.

examples.title: Seeing your face at seventy
examples.text: In 2011 Hershfield and colleagues, including Stanford's Jeremy Bailenson, had working-age adults interact in virtual reality with a realistic, age-progressed rendering of themselves. Those who did allocated a significantly higher share of hypothetical income to retirement saving than those who saw their current face. NYU Stern's summary reports approximately 33 percent more. The authors found that feeling more continuous with the future self helped explain the effect. A caution from one review: in the first of the paper's studies the undergraduate result was not statistically significant.

examples.title: Brain scans and the discounting of rewards
examples.text: In a 2009 brain-imaging study at Stanford, Ersner-Hershfield, Wimmer and Knutson scanned participants while they rated how well traits described their current self and their future self. Differences in activity in the rostral anterior cingulate cortex between the two kinds of judgement predicted how steeply the same people discounted future rewards when tested a week later. In other words, how the brain treats the future self predicted real choices between now and later, as Parfit's picture would suggest.

examples.title: Parfit's own glass tunnel
examples.text: Parfit described the effect of his own philosophy on his daily experience. Before he changed his view, he said, his life seemed like a glass tunnel through which he was moving faster every year, at the end of which was darkness. After the change, the walls of the tunnel disappeared, and he lived in the open air, with less concern for the rest of his own life and more for the lives of others. It is a first-person report, not an experiment, but it shows the idea being lived rather than only argued.

images.caption: Derek Parfit at Harvard in April 2015.
images.credit: Anna Riedl / CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

why: Philosophically it is a minority but influential view; the empirical work (an fMRI study, a self-report index and virtual-reality experiments) supports a link between feeling connected to your future self and saving, but some of it is correlational.
Caveat: most of the experiments use small samples or hypothetical allocations, and one of the age-progression studies was not significant on its own.
ideas.try_this: Write a short, kind note to yourself at 70, or imagine a specific day in their life, and then choose one thing you'll do this week for them, such as a pension top-up or a health check.

ideas.title: A famine that echoed through DNA
ideas.idea: Between November 1944 and May 1945, the western Netherlands endured the Hunger Winter, when rations fell to between 400 and 800 calories a day. The famine began and ended abruptly, and Dutch records were excellent, which accidentally created one of the cleanest natural experiments in human biology. Scientists have since followed people who were in the womb at the time. Six decades later, those exposed around the time of conception carried a measurable chemical mark on a growth-related gene, IGF2, that their unexposed brothers and sisters did not. It is a mark on how the gene is switched, not a change to the genetic code. The finding helped show that early conditions can leave a molecular trace that lasts a lifetime, and it changed how we think about nature versus nurture: they are not two separate things.
ideas.deep_dive:
The Dutch famine ran from November 1944 to May 1945 in the occupied west of the country. According to the Oregon Health & Science University's page on the Dutch Famine Birth Cohort, about 20,000 people died and 4.5 million were affected, with rations of 400 to 800 calories a day. When food returned in the spring of 1945, the shock ended as sharply as it had begun. That clear start and end date is what makes the famine so useful to scientists: anyone born in a given window can be placed precisely on a timeline of exposure.

Early studies of the people born during and after the famine found that its effects depended on when in pregnancy the mother was starved. Later work turned to the mechanism. In 2008 Bastiaan Heijmans and colleagues compared 60 people conceived during the famine with their same-sex siblings, who had not been exposed. Six decades on, the exposed group had less DNA methylation, a chemical tag that helps control whether a gene is active, near the imprinted gene IGF2. The difference appeared with exposure around conception, not in late gestation.

The finding needs careful reading. A follow-up study in PLoS ONE (2012) reported small effect sizes, under 3% in absolute terms. These tags are not a code that dictates health; they are one of many ways early life leaves a trace. Their health consequences in this cohort are still debated, and the work concerns people exposed to extreme starvation, not ordinary variations in diet. Nor does this show the effects are inherited by later generations; that is a separate and more contested question.

examples.title: Brothers and sisters as the control group
examples.text: Heijmans and colleagues' 2008 study in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences compared 60 people conceived during the Hunger Winter with their same-sex siblings. Because brothers and sisters share much of their genes and family background, any consistent difference is more likely to come from the famine. The exposed group had lower methylation of IGF2 six decades later, but only when exposure was around conception. The sibling design is a model for how to find a signal in messy human data.

examples.title: Famine and body weight at 18
examples.text: Conti and colleagues (2024, Economics & Human Biology) used military recruit data to study Dutch men born around the famine. They found that those exposed since early gestation had a higher body mass index and a greater chance of being overweight at age 18. The authors also found that selection and scarring both matter: because the weakest fetuses may not have survived, the people measured are not a random sample. It shows how a starving mother can shape her child's later metabolism.

examples.title: A smaller-effect follow-up
examples.text: In 2012 a team re-examined the same 60 sibling pairs in PLoS ONE, measuring five regions of IGF2 and H19. They found small but consistent differences in methylation at all IGF2 regions but not at H19, with absolute effects under 3%. A separate analysis of 15 loci found changes at six of them. A good example of the scientific process: the first striking result held up, but at a much more modest scale than headlines implied.

why: The famine's sharp start and end, plus sibling comparisons, make this unusually strong evidence for human prenatal programming; the IGF2 result comes from 60 pairs and was followed up in a second paper.
Caveat: the methylation differences are small, and their effect on health is not settled. Extreme starvation is not a model for ordinary diets.
ideas.try_this: Think about which of your own habits or health risks you put down to 'genes' or to 'choices'. What would a third factor, such as early conditions you can't remember, change about how you judge them?
